claim: Gap genes mediate the division of the anterior-posterior axis of insects into different fates through regulating downstream hox genes.
source: Gap genes mediate the division of the anterior-posterior axis of insects into different fates through regulating downstream hox genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general statement about gap gene function.

claim: Gap genes in Drosophila melanogaster are regulated (at least initially) through a threshold-based mechanism, guided by both anteriorly- and posteriorly-localized morphogen gradients.
source: Decades of tinkering the segmentation gene network of Drosophila melanogaster led to the conclusion that gap genes are regulated (at least initially) through a threshold-based mechanism, guided by both anteriorly- and posteriorly-localized morphogen gradients.
evidence: This claim is based on decades of research on Drosophila segmentation, as stated in the abstract.

claim: The response of the gap gene network in Tribolium castaneum upon perturbation is consistent with a threshold-free 'Speed Regulation' mechanism.
source: In this paper, we show that the response of the gap gene network in the beetle Tribolium castaneum upon perturbation is consistent with a threshold-free 'Speed Regulation' mechanism, in which the speed of a genetic cascade of gap genes is regulated by a posterior morphogen gradient.
evidence: This is the main finding of the paper, supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: In the Speed Regulation mechanism, the speed of a genetic cascade of gap genes is regulated by a posterior morphogen gradient.
source: In this paper, we show that the response of the gap gene network in the beetle Tribolium castaneum upon perturbation is consistent with a threshold-free 'Speed Regulation' mechanism, in which the speed of a genetic cascade of gap genes is regulated by a posterior morphogen gradient.
evidence: This describes the core mechanism of the Speed Regulation model as stated in the abstract.

claim: Re-inducing hunchback results in the re-induction of the gap gene cascade at arbitrary points in time in Tribolium castaneum.
source: We show this by re-inducing the leading gap gene (namely, hunchback) resulting in the re-induction of the gap gene cascade at arbitrary points in time.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in the paper using heat-shock experiments.

claim: The gap gene network is self-regulatory and is primarily under the control of a posterior regulator in Tribolium.
source: This demonstrates that the gap gene network is self-regulatory and is primarily under the control of a posterior regulator in Tribolium and possibly other short/intermediate-germ insects.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental results showing re-induction of the gap gene cascade.

claim: The gap gene network may be self-regulatory and primarily under the control of a posterior regulator in other short/intermediate-germ insects.
source: This demonstrates that the gap gene network is self-regulatory and is primarily under the control of a posterior regulator in Tribolium and possibly other short/intermediate-germ insects.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings in Tribolium to other insects.

claim: The French Flag model is one of the earliest models of pattern formation in development.
source: The French Flag model is one of the earliest models of pattern formation in development (Wolpert, 1969), in which thresholds of a morphogen gradient (e.g. T1 and T2 in Figure 1A') set the boundaries between different gene expression domains.
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citation to Wolpert, 1969.

claim: In the French Flag model, thresholds of a morphogen gradient set the boundaries between different gene expression domains.
source: The French Flag model is one of the earliest models of pattern formation in development (Wolpert, 1969), in which thresholds of a morphogen gradient (e.g. T1 and T2 in Figure 1A') set the boundaries between different gene expression domains.
evidence: This describes the core mechanism of the French Flag model, illustrated in Figure 1A'.

claim: Gene expression domains are usually found to be dynamic.
source: First, gene expression domains are usually found to be dynamic, and in many cases, are expressed sequentially in a wave-like fashion (e.g. during neural tube and limb bud patterning in vertebrates and during anterior-posterior (AP) fate specification in vertebrates and insects) (Briscoe and Small, 2015; Panovska-Griffiths et al., 2013; Cohen et al., 2014; Balaskas et al., 2012; Dessaud et al., 2007; Zeller, 2004; Harfe et al., 2004; El-Sherif et al., 2014; El-Sherif et al., 2012a; Zhu et al., 2017; Kuhlmann and El-Sherif, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies showing dynamic gene expression patterns.

claim: Gene expression domains are in many cases expressed sequentially in a wave-like fashion during neural tube and limb bud patterning in vertebrates and during anterior-posterior fate specification in vertebrates and insects.
source: First, gene expression domains are usually found to be dynamic, and in many cases, are expressed sequentially in a wave-like fashion (e.g. during neural tube and limb bud patterning in vertebrates and during anterior-posterior (AP) fate specification in vertebrates and insects) (Briscoe and Small, 2015; Panovska-Griffiths et al., 2013; Cohen et al., 2014; Balaskas et al., 2012; Dessaud et al., 2007; Zeller, 2004; Harfe et al., 2004; El-Sherif et al., 2014; El-Sherif et al., 2012a; Zhu et al., 2017; Kuhlmann and El-Sherif, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies in vertebrates and insects.

claim: Even if activated simultaneously, gene expression domains usually undergo continuous shifts in space.
source: Even if activated simultaneously, gene expression domains usually undergo continuous shifts in space (e.g. gap and pair-rule domains in Drosophila) (El-Sherif and Levine, 2016; Verd et al., 2018; Jaeger et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Drosophila gap and pair-rule genes.

claim: It is difficult to correlate the locations of gene expression domains with specific values of morphogen concentrations when gene expression domains are dynamic.
source: In such cases, it is difficult to correlate the locations of gene expression domains with specific values of morphogen concentrations.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that gene expression domains are dynamic.

claim: Morphogen exposure time has a crucial effect on patterning.
source: Second, morphogen exposure time was found to have a crucial effect on patterning.
evidence: This is supported by examples provided in the following sentences with citations.

claim: The exposure time of Caudal regulates the timing of gap and pair-rule genes in insects.
source: For example, the exposure time of Caudal (Cad) regulates the timing of gap and pair-rule genes in insects and that of Hox genes in vertebrates (Zhu et al., 2017; Neijts et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2017 and Neijts et al., 2017.

claim: The exposure time of Caudal regulates the timing of Hox genes in vertebrates.
source: For example, the exposure time of Caudal (Cad) regulates the timing of gap and pair-rule genes in insects and that of Hox genes in vertebrates (Zhu et al., 2017; Neijts et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2017 and Neijts et al., 2017.

claim: The concentration and exposure time of Sonic hedgehog determines which fate a cell in the vertebrate neural tube and limb bud will take.
source: Similarly, the concentration and exposure time of Sonic hedgehog (Shh) determines which fate a cell in the vertebrate neural tube and limb bud will take (Dessaud et al., 2007; Zeller, 2004; Harfe et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Sonic hedgehog signaling.

claim: Recent works in morphogen-mediated patterning are suggesting a more dynamic and time-based paradigm rather than threshold-based.
source: For these reasons, recent works in morphogen-mediated patterning are suggesting a more dynamic and time-based paradigm rather than threshold-based (Briscoe and Small, 2015; Dessaud et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2017; Verd et al., 2018; Jaeger et al., 2004; Verd et al., 2017; Clark, 2017; Clark and Akam, 2016; Clark and Peel, 2018; Brena and Akam, 2013; García-Solache et al., 2010; Chipman and Akam, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: The general description of the French Flag model is purely phenomenological.
source: However, the general description of the French Flag model (Wolpert, 1969) (Figure 1A,A') is purely phenomenological (i.e. descriptive).
evidence: This is an assessment of the nature of the French Flag model as originally described.

claim: Important classes of GRN realization of the French Flag model 'transiently' exhibit dynamic gene expression domains and sensitivity to morphogen exposure times.
source: In this paper, we show that indeed important classes of GRN realization of the French Flag model 'transiently' exhibit exactly these features.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling in the paper.

claim: At an initial transient phase, gene expression domains in French Flag GRN realizations are dynamic and keep shifting and shrinking as long as the morphogen gradient is applied.
source: In particular, at an initial transient phase, gene expression domains are dynamic and keep shifting and shrinking as long as the morphogen gradient is applied, hence its sensitivity to the exposure time of the morphogen gradient.
evidence: This is shown through computational modeling in the paper.

claim: Gene expression domains in French Flag GRN realizations finally stabilize at the thresholds set by the morphogen gradient.
source: However, gene expression domains finally stabilize at the thresholds set by the morphogen gradient, adhering to the tenets of the French Flag model.
evidence: This is shown through computational modeling in the paper.

claim: The defining feature of the French Flag model is its threshold-based steady state behavior.
source: Hence, we argue that the defining feature of the French Flag model is not its transient dynamics, but its threshold-based steady state behavior.
evidence: This is an argument made by the authors based on their analysis of French Flag GRN realizations.

claim: The Speed Regulation model is purely time-based and threshold-free.
source: However, a recently devised mechanism (termed 'Speed Regulation' model, Figure 1B,B') (Zhu et al., 2017; Kuhlmann and El-Sherif, 2018), that has been suggested to be the basis of the AP fate specification in insects, is purely time-based and threshold-free (by 'threshold' we mean thresholds of the morphogen gradient, not other possible thresholds in the cross-regulatory interactions between patterning genes).
evidence: This is a description of the Speed Regulation model from cited literature.

claim: In the Speed Regulation model, segmentation genes of the gap class are wired into a genetic cascade, so that gap genes are activated sequentially in time.
source: In this model, segmentation genes of the gap class are wired into a genetic cascade, so that gap genes are activated sequentially in time.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the Speed Regulation model.

claim: The temporal progression of gap gene expressions is translated into a spatial pattern through modulating the speed of the gap gene cascade by a morphogen gradient of caudal.
source: The temporal progression of gap gene expressions is translated into a spatial pattern through modulating the speed (or timing) of the gap gene cascade by a morphogen gradient of the transcription factor caudal (cad) (or of factor(s) which expression correlate with that of cad).
evidence: This describes how the Speed Regulation model works.

claim: In the Speed Regulation model, gene expression domains keep shifting and shrinking as long as the morphogen gradient is applied until the gradient is retracted.
source: In contrast to the French Flag model, the Speed Regulation model is completely threshold-free, where gene expression domains keep shifting and shrinking as long as the morphogen gradient is applied (without ever reaching a steady state) until the gradient is retracted.
evidence: This is a key distinguishing feature of the Speed Regulation model.

claim: Re-inducing hunchback at arbitrary times during the AP specification phase of Tribolium castaneum resulted in resetting the gap gene cascade and re-establishing the gap gene expression sequence in time and space.
source: In this paper, to demonstrate the threshold-free nature of gap gene regulation, we re-induce the leading gene in the gap gene cascade (namely, hunchback, hb) at arbitrary times during the AP specification phase of the beetle Tribolium castaneum using a transgenic line carrying a heat-shock-driven hb CDS. This resulted in resetting the gap gene cascade and re-establishing the gap gene expression sequence in time and space.
evidence: This is the main experimental finding of the paper.

claim: The self-regulatory behavior of gap gene regulation argues against the existence of a spatial or temporal signal that sets the locations of gap gene expression boundaries in a threshold-based fashion.
source: This argues against the existence of a spatial or temporal signal that sets the locations of gap gene expression boundaries in a threshold-based fashion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The self-regulatory behavior of gap gene regulation is difficult to explain using the French Flag model.
source: Using computational modeling, we show that this self-regulatory behavior of gap gene regulation is difficult to explain using the French Flag model and, alternatively, is indicative of time-based (or 'speed regulation'-based) patterning.
evidence: This is shown through computational modeling in the paper.

claim: The self-regulatory behavior of gap gene regulation is indicative of time-based (or 'speed regulation'-based) patterning.
source: Using computational modeling, we show that this self-regulatory behavior of gap gene regulation is difficult to explain using the French Flag model and, alternatively, is indicative of time-based (or 'speed regulation'-based) patterning.
evidence: This is shown through computational modeling in the paper.

claim: The basic French Flag model is incapable of reproducing the phenomenology of insect development and evolution.
source: We argue that the basic French Flag model, in contrast to the Speed Regulation model, is incapable of reproducing the phenomenology of insect development and evolution.
evidence: This is an argument made by the authors based on their analysis.

claim: The major difference between the French Flag model and the Speed Regulation model is that the French Flag model depends on morphogen thresholds in setting the boundaries between gene expression domains, whereas the Speed Regulation model is self-regulatory and threshold-free.
source: We show that the major difference between the two models is that the French Flag model (and its modified version) depends on morphogen thresholds in setting the boundaries between gene expression domains, whereas the Speed Regulation model is self-regulatory and threshold-free.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the theoretical analysis in the paper.

claim: An experimental test to differentiate between French Flag and Speed Regulation models is whether the patterning scheme can be reset independently from any temporal or positional signal.
source: We suggest an experimental test to differentiate between the two mechanisms: whether the patterning scheme can be reset independently from any temporal or positional signal.
evidence: This is the experimental test proposed and carried out in the paper.

claim: The Speed Regulation model is a more plausible mechanism to explain insect development and evolution.
source: We then carry out this test experimentally in the beetle Tribolium castaneum, concluding that the Speed Regulation model is a more plausible mechanism to explain insect development and evolution.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper based on experimental results.

claim: In the French Flag GRN, the morphogen gradient activates different genes with different strengths.
source: In the example GRN in Figure 1A'', the morphogen gradient (grey) activates different genes with different strengths: strongly activates the blue gene, moderately activates the red gene, and weakly activates the green gene.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the French Flag GRN shown in Figure 1A''.

claim: Cross-regulatory interaction between genes further delimit gene expression bands in the French Flag GRN.
source: Cross-regulatory interaction between genes further delimit gene expression bands (See Appendix 1 for description of how the FF GRN in Figure 1A'' works; see simulation of a 5-genes FF GRN in Figure 1C, Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This describes how the French Flag GRN works, with reference to figures and videos.

claim: In the Speed Regulation GRN realization, two GRN modules are employed: a dynamic module and a static module.
source: In this realization, two GRN modules are employed: a dynamic module and a static module (see Figure 1B'' for a 3-genes realization and Appendix 1 for a 5-genes realization).
evidence: This describes the structure of the Speed Regulation GRN.

claim: The dynamic module in the Speed Regulation GRN is a genetic cascade that mediates the sequential activation of its constituent genes.
source: The dynamic module is a genetic cascade that mediates the sequential activation of its constituent genes.
evidence: This describes the function of the dynamic module in the Speed Regulation GRN.

claim: The static module in the Speed Regulation GRN is a multi-stable network that mediates the refinement and stabilization of gene expression patterns.
source: The static module is a multi-stable network that mediates the refinement and stabilization of gene expression patterns.
evidence: This describes the function of the static module in the Speed Regulation GRN.

claim: In the Speed Regulation GRN, the morphogen gradient activates the dynamic but represses the static module.
source: The morphogen gradient activates the dynamic but represses the static module.
evidence: This describes how the morphogen gradient regulates the two modules in the Speed Regulation GRN.

claim: As we go from high to low values of the morphogen gradient, the dynamic module experiences excessively higher stabilizing effect from the static module, and consequently, runs slower.
source: Hence, as we go from high to low values of the morphogen gradient, the dynamic module experiences excessively higher stabilizing effect from the static module, and consequently, runs slower.
evidence: This explains how the Speed Regulation mechanism works in the GRN realization.

claim: Gene expression domains in the French Flag model are only dynamic during the initial transient phase, but eventually reach a steady state where they stabilize at certain morphogen thresholds.
source: A main difference, however, is that gene expression domains in the FF model realizations are only dynamic during the initial transient phase, but eventually reach a steady state where they stabilize at certain morphogen thresholds (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This is shown through computational modeling in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Video 1.

claim: Gene expression domains in the Speed Regulation model keep shrinking and propagating towards the low end of the morphogen and never stabilize or reach a steady state, unless the morphogen gradient decays or retracts.
source: On the other hand, gene expression domains in the SR model keep shrinking and propagating towards the low end of the morphogen and never stabilize or reach a steady state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Video 3), unless the morphogen gradient decays or retracts (Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: This is shown through computational modeling in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Videos 3-5.

claim: The anterior fates of insects form in a non-growing tissue called the 'blastoderm'.
source: The anterior fates of insects (Figure 2A) form in a non-growing tissue (called the 'blastoderm'), whereas posterior fates form in a growing tissue (called the 'germband') (Davis and Patel, 2002; El-Sherif et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is a description of insect development supported by citations.

claim: The posterior fates of insects form in a growing tissue called the 'germband'.
source: The anterior fates of insects (Figure 2A) form in a non-growing tissue (called the 'blastoderm'), whereas posterior fates form in a growing tissue (called the 'germband') (Davis and Patel, 2002; El-Sherif et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is a description of insect development supported by citations.

claim: In short-germ insects, most of AP fates are specified in the germband.
source: In short-germ insects, (most of) AP fates are specified in the germband (first column in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a description of short-germ insect development illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: In long-germ insects, most of AP fates form in the blastoderm before transiting into the germband stage.
source: In long-germ insects, (most of) AP fates form in the blastoderm before transiting into the germband stage (third column in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a description of long-germ insect development illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Intermediate-germ insects lie somewhere in between short-germ and long-germ insects, where several fates are specified in the blastoderm, and the rest in the germband.
source: Intermediate-germ insects lie somewhere in between these two extreme cases, where several fates are specified in the blastoderm, and the rest in the germband (second column in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a description of intermediate-germ insect development illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Throughout evolution, the specification of AP fates seems to shift easily from the germband to the blastoderm, resulting in a trend of short-germ to long-germ evolution.
source: Throughout evolution, the specification of AP fates seems to shift easily from the germband to the blastoderm, resulting in a trend of short-germ to long-germ evolution (Davis and Patel, 2002; Peel et al., 2005; Peel, 2004).
evidence: This is an evolutionary observation supported by citations.

claim: AP fate specification in short- and intermediate-germ insects is mediated by the Speed Regulation model, where a posterior morphogen regulates the sequential activation of the AP-determinant genes of the gap class.
source: In ref (Zhu et al., 2017), it was suggested that AP fate specification in short- and intermediate-germ insects is mediated by the SR model, where a posterior morphogen (cad in Tribolium, or some other graded factor which expression correlates with that of cad) regulates the sequential activation of the AP-determinant genes of the gap class.
evidence: This is a suggestion from previous work cited in the paper.

claim: The Speed Regulation model can operate in a gradient-based mode, which can pattern a non-elongating tissue.
source: This suggestion was based on the observation that the SR model can operate in two modes (Figure 2B): a gradient-based, which can pattern a non-elongating tissue (as discussed in the previous section), and a wavefront-based mode in which the posterior morphogen gradient continuously retracts as the tissue elongates, in a set-up similar to the Clock-and-Wavefront model (Pourquié, 2003; Palmeirim et al., 1997; Dubrulle et al., 2001; Lauschke et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the two modes of operation of the Speed Regulation model.

claim: The Speed Regulation model can operate in a wavefront-based mode in which the posterior morphogen gradient continuously retracts as the tissue elongates.
source: This suggestion was based on the observation that the SR model can operate in two modes (Figure 2B): a gradient-based, which can pattern a non-elongating tissue (as discussed in the previous section), and a wavefront-based mode in which the posterior morphogen gradient continuously retracts as the tissue elongates, in a set-up similar to the Clock-and-Wavefront model (Pourquié, 2003; Palmeirim et al., 1997; Dubrulle et al., 2001; Lauschke et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the wavefront-based mode of the Speed Regulation model.

claim: The flexibility of the Speed Regulation model to pattern both elongating and non-elongating tissues could offer an evolutionary mechanism where a smooth transition between short- and long-germ modes of insect development is possible.
source: It was also shown that the flexibility of the SR model to pattern both elongating and non-elongating tissues could offer an evolutionary mechanism where a smooth transition between short- and long-germ modes of insect development is possible (Video 6).
evidence: This is shown through computational modeling in Video 6.

claim: In the French Flag with a Timer Gene model, the posterior morphogen activates a Timer Gene.
source: In this scheme, the posterior morphogen (fourth column in Figure 2A, and grey in Figure 2C) activates a gene (termed a 'Timer Gene' (François and Siggia, 2010); fifth column in Figure 2A, and black in Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the French Flag with a Timer Gene model.

claim: The Timer Gene is assumed to have negligible decay rate, so that it continuously builds up in a non-growing tissue.
source: The Timer Gene is assumed to have negligible decay rate, so that it continuously builds up in a non-growing tissue (left column in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an assumption of the French Flag with a Timer Gene model.

claim: In a growing tissue, the expression of the Timer Gene builds up in the presence of the retracting posterior gradient, while it stabilizes upon its retraction.
source: In a growing tissue, the expression of the Timer Gene (black in Figure 2C, right column) builds up in the presence of the retracting posterior gradient (grey in Figure 2C, right column), while it stabilizes upon its retraction.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the Timer Gene in a growing tissue.

claim: A long-range gradient of the Timer Gene forms along the whole axis of the full-grown tissue.
source: Hence, a long-range gradient of the Timer Gene forms along the whole axis of the full-grown tissue (last row in the fifth column of Figure 2A and the right column of Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a consequence of the Timer Gene dynamics described.

claim: Thresholds of different concentrations of the Timer Gene set the boundaries between different fates.
source: Thresholds of different concentrations of the Timer Gene then set the boundaries between different fates, in a similar fashion to the FF model (thresholds are shown in arrows in Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes how the Timer Gene sets boundaries in the French Flag with a Timer Gene model.

claim: Both the Speed Regulation model and the French Flag with a Timer Gene model can operate in gradient-based and wavefront-based modes and exhibit similar dynamics and final pattern.
source: We notice that both the SR model and the FFTG model can operate in gradient-based and wavefront-based modes (and, hence, can pattern both non-elongating and elongating tissues) and exhibit similar dynamics and final pattern (compare Figure 2B and C; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown through comparison of computational models in figures.

claim: A transition from a gradient-based to wavefront-based patterning would still result in a long-range gradient of the Timer Gene along the tissue axis.
source: A transition from a gradient-based to wavefront-based patterning would still result in a long-range gradient of the Timer Gene along the tissue axis (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Similar to the Speed Regulation model, the French Flag with a Timer Gene model can mediate AP fate specification in insects of different germ types.
source: Hence, similar to the SR model, the FFTG model can mediate AP fate specification in insects of different germ types: operating in the wavefront-based mode for short-germ insects, operating in the gradient-based mode for long-germ insects, and operating in the gradient-based then switching to wavefront-based mode for intermediate-germ insects (Video 7; compare to Video 6).
evidence: This is shown through computational modeling in Video 7.

claim: The sequential activation of genes in the Speed Regulation model is mediated by the interaction between the fate-specifying genes themselves.
source: Here, we note that the sequential activation of genes in the SR model is mediated by the interaction between the fate-specifying genes themselves, whereas the Timer Gene is the mediator of sequential gene activation in the FFTG model.
evidence: This is a key difference between the two models.

claim: The Timer Gene is the mediator of sequential gene activation in the French Flag with a Timer Gene model.
source: Here, we note that the sequential activation of genes in the SR model is mediated by the interaction between the fate-specifying genes themselves, whereas the Timer Gene is the mediator of sequential gene activation in the FFTG model.
evidence: This is a key difference between the two models.

claim: Force-resetting the fate-specification gene sequence will reset the Speed Regulation model.
source: Hence, force-resetting the fate-specification gene sequence will reset the SR model, whereas resetting the expression pattern for the FFTG model would require resetting the Timer Gene instead.
evidence: This is a prediction from the structure of the Speed Regulation model.

claim: Resetting the expression pattern for the French Flag with a Timer Gene model would require resetting the Timer Gene.
source: Hence, force-resetting the fate-specification gene sequence will reset the SR model, whereas resetting the expression pattern for the FFTG model would require resetting the Timer Gene instead.
evidence: This is a prediction from the structure of the French Flag with a Timer Gene model.

claim: In the French Flag with a Timer Gene model, the blue gene becomes briefly dominant after re-induction, but the already formed pattern and the newly forming pattern are largely unchanged.
source: In the FFTG model, the blue gene becomes briefly dominant, but the already formed pattern and the newly forming pattern are largely unchanged (compare 5th to 3rd column of Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown through computational modeling in Figure 2E.

claim: Re-inducing the blue gene in the Speed Regulation model results in the deletion of the already formed pattern outside of the expression domain of the posterior morphogen and the re-establishment of the temporal gene sequence within the expression of the posterior morphogen.
source: On the other hand, re-inducing the blue gene had two consequences in the case of our GRN realization of the SR model (compare 4th and 6th columns of Figure 2E): (i) the already formed pattern outside of the expression domain of the posterior morphogen is deleted and dominated by the continued expression of the blue gene, and (ii) the temporal gene sequence is re-established within the expression of the posterior morphogen, resulting in the re-establishment of the patterning process.
evidence: This is shown through computational modeling in Figure 2E.

claim: During AP patterning of the Tribolium embryo, gap genes are expressed in sequential waves of gene expressions that propagate from posterior to anterior in the presence of a gradient of caudal.
source: During AP patterning of the Tribolium embryo, gap genes (namely, hunchback (hb), Krüppel (Kr), milles-pattes (mlpt), and giant (gt); Figure 3) (Bucher and Klingler, 2004; Wolff et al., 1998; Savard et al., 2006; Cerny et al., 2005; Marques-Souza, 2007) are expressed in sequential waves of gene expressions that propagate from posterior to anterior in the presence of a gradient of the master regulator caudal (cad) (based on a correlational evidence, however) (Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of gap gene expression in Tribolium supported by citations and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Upon retraction of the cad gradient, gap gene expressions stabilize into static domains before they gradually fade.
source: Upon retraction of the cad gradient, gap gene expressions stabilize into static domains before they gradually fade.
evidence: This describes the behavior of gap genes after cad retraction.

claim: Some of the gap genes have two trunk expression domains, namely: hb, mlpt and gt.
source: Some of the gap genes have two trunk expression domains, namely: hb, mlpt and gt (shown in blue, green and gold, respectively in Figure 3; late trunk domains are outlined in black).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: Briefly heat-shocking hs-hb embryos at 26–29 hr After Egg Lay resulted in a ubiquitous expression of hb that lasted for 6 hr post heat-shock.
source: Briefly heat-shocking hs-hb embryos at 26–29 hr After Egg Lay (AEL) indeed resulted in a ubiquitous expression of hb that lasted for 6 hr post heat-shock (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; for a basic description of the cuticular and morphological phenotypes of heat-shocked hs-hb embryos, see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Heat-shocking WT embryos at 26–29 hr AEL resulted in a normal progression of gap gene expression, albeit with an initial delay of around 9 hr, compared to non-heat-shocked WT embryos.
source: As a control, we also heat-shocked WT embryos at 26–29 hr AEL, and noticed a normal progression of gap gene expression, albeit with an initial delay of around 9 hr, compared to non-heat-shocked WT embryos (compare Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 to Figure 3; see also Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figures 4A, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells in hs-hb embryos had two distinct responses depending on whether they are within or anterior to the active-zone.
source: We observed that cells in hs-hb embryos had two distinct responses depending on whether they are within or anterior to the active-zone.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Gene expression domains anterior to the active-zone are pre-maturely repressed in heat-shocked hs-hb embryos, compared to heat-shocked WT.
source: Gene expression domains anterior to the active-zone are pre-maturely repressed, compared to heat-shocked WT.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Within the active-zone, the gap gene domains sequence is re-induced in heat-shocked hs-hb embryos, and eventually propagates towards anterior.
source: Within the active-zone, the gap gene domains sequence is re-induced, and eventually propagates towards anterior (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In heat-shocked hs-hb embryos, at around 35–38 hr AEL, Kr expression anterior to the active-zone was down-regulated.
source: Specifically, in heat-shocked hs-hb embryos, at around 35–38 hr AEL, Kr expression anterior to the active-zone was down-regulated (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At around 41 hr AEL, Kr expression was re-initiated in the active-zone of heat-shocked hs-hb embryos, an effect that is not noticed in heat-shocked WT embryos.
source: At around 41 hr AEL, Kr expression was re-initiated in the active-zone of heat-shocked hs-hb embryos, an effect that is not noticed in heat-shocked WT embryos (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The re-initiated Kr expression then propagated towards anterior in heat-shocked hs-hb embryos.
source: The re-initiated Kr expression then propagated towards anterior.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: At 35 hr AEL, the already established mlpt expression at the anterior of hs-hb embryos was down-regulated.
source: A similar effect is observed for the gap gene mlpt. At 35 hr AEL, the already established mlpt expression at the anterior of hs-hb embryos was down-regulated.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: By 41 hr AEL, mlpt expression was re-established in the active-zone and propagated towards anterior in heat-shocked hs-hb embryos.
source: By 41 hr AEL, mlpt expression was re-established in the active-zone and propagated towards anterior.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The second domain of the re-established mlpt expression appeared at 56 hr AEL in heat-shocked hs-hb embryos.
source: The second domain of the re-established mlpt expression appeared at 56 hr AEL.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The already formed two domains of gt expression were repressed in the anterior and new two domains of expressions were re-established in the posterior of hs-hb embryos that eventually propagated towards anterior.
source: Similarly, the already formed two domains of gt expression were repressed in the anterior and new two domains of expressions were re-established in the posterior of hs-hb embryos that eventually propagated towards anterior (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In HS Anterior cells, gap genes are pre-maturely down-regulated upon re-inducing hb.
source: In HS Anterior cells, gap genes are pre-maturely down-regulated; while within the Active-Zone, gap gene sequence is re-induced and eventually propagates towards the Anterior region (as shown in HS Anterior, Active-Zone, and Anterior, respectively in Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown through quantification in Figure 4C.

claim: Within the Active-Zone, gap gene sequence is re-induced and eventually propagates towards the Anterior region upon re-inducing hb.
source: In HS Anterior cells, gap genes are pre-maturely down-regulated; while within the Active-Zone, gap gene sequence is re-induced and eventually propagates towards the Anterior region (as shown in HS Anterior, Active-Zone, and Anterior, respectively in Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown through quantification in Figure 4C.

claim: In WT, starting from 14 hr AEL, hb, Kr, mlpt and gt expression domains arise sequentially in the active-zone.
source: It is worth noting here that, in WT, starting from 14 hr AEL, hb, Kr, mlpt and gt expression domains arise sequentially in the active-zone (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: By 26 hr AEL, the majority of gap gene expression domains already propagated out of the active-zone towards anterior, and the active-zone becomes virtually void of any gap gene expression.
source: By 26 hr AEL, the majority of gap gene expression domains already propagated out of the active-zone towards anterior, and the active-zone becomes virtually void of any gap gene expression.
evidence: This is a description of gap gene expression dynamics in WT.

claim: Around 29 hr AEL, the second abdominal domains of mlpt and hb arise in the active-zone.
source: Around 29 hr AEL, the second abdominal domains of mlpt and hb arise in the active-zone (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: The fact that the entire gap gene sequence is re-induced upon re-inducing hb in the active-zone at a point in time and space where gap genes are not expressed in WT indicates that gap genes are wired into an 'aperiodic' clock that can be reset at any point in time.
source: The fact that the entire gap gene sequence is re-induced upon re-inducing hb in the active-zone at a point in time and space where gap genes are not expressed in WT indicates that gap genes are wired into an 'aperiodic' clock that can be reset at any point in time and strongly argues against a threshold-based French Flag model underlying gap gene regulation in Tribolium and is consistent with a mechanism based on the Speed Regulation model, as discussed in our earlier theoretical analysis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The re-induction of the gap gene sequence upon re-inducing hb strongly argues against a threshold-based French Flag model underlying gap gene regulation in Tribolium.
source: The fact that the entire gap gene sequence is re-induced upon re-inducing hb in the active-zone at a point in time and space where gap genes are not expressed in WT indicates that gap genes are wired into an 'aperiodic' clock that can be reset at any point in time and strongly argues against a threshold-based French Flag model underlying gap gene regulation in Tribolium and is consistent with a mechanism based on the Speed Regulation model, as discussed in our earlier theoretical analysis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The re-induction of the gap gene sequence upon re-inducing hb is consistent with a mechanism based on the Speed Regulation model.
source: The fact that the entire gap gene sequence is re-induced upon re-inducing hb in the active-zone at a point in time and space where gap genes are not expressed in WT indicates that gap genes are wired into an 'aperiodic' clock that can be reset at any point in time and strongly argues against a threshold-based French Flag model underlying gap gene regulation in Tribolium and is consistent with a mechanism based on the Speed Regulation model, as discussed in our earlier theoretical analysis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The dual response of the Tribolium embryo to the re-induction of hb provides an indirect support for the two-modules GRN realization of the Speed Regulation model.
source: Furthermore, the dual response of the Tribolium embryo to the re-induction of hb provides an indirect support for the two-modules GRN realization of the SR model (Figure 1B'').
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The difference in response between the active-zone and anterior cells can be explained by a difference in the genetic wiring of gap genes in these two regions, encoded by two different GRNs.
source: The difference in response between the active-zone and anterior cells can be explained by a difference in the genetic wiring of gap genes in these two regions, encoded by two different GRNs (e.g. dynamic and static modules).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: For heat-shock experiments at time windows 23–26 hr AEL and 20–23 hr AEL, the expression within the active-zone suffered a transient down-regulation before the gap gene sequence is re-induced.
source: For both time windows, the expression within the active-zone suffered a transient down-regulation before the gap gene sequence is re-induced.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from heat-shock experiments at different time windows.

claim: The transient down-regulation before re-induction indicates that the gap gene clock is based on a genetic cascade with mutual-repressive links.
source: This indicates that the gap gene clock is based on a genetic cascade with mutual-repressive links, like the one we used in our theoretical analysis (dynamic module in Figure 1B'').
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The difference in response to the re-induction of hb between the active-zone and the anterior supports the module switching model and disfavors a degradation rate modulation model.
source: As discussed above, the difference in response to the re-induction of hb between the active-zone and the anterior supports the module switching model (and disfavors a degradation rate modulation model; Video 11).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and computational modeling.

claim: In axn RNAi embryos, the cad gradient extends to cover most of the embryo, transforming the embryo into an enlarged active-zone.
source: To this end, we utilized the axin (axn) RNAi phenotype in Tribolium, where the cad gradient extends to cover most of the embryo, transforming the embryo into an enlarged active-zone (albeit still expressed in a gradient; Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Zhu et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the axn RNAi phenotype supported by citations and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In axn RNAi embryos, mlpt expression proceeded as in WT but propagated across the whole embryo and never stabilized.
source: In axn RNAi embryos, mlpt expression proceeded as in WT but propagated across the whole embryo and never stabilized, consistent with the fact that the whole embryo transformed into an active-zone (Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an experimental observation consistent with previous findings.

claim: In hs-hb; axn RNAi embryos, after a transient down-regulation of mlpt expression, mlpt expression emerged at the posterior then expanded to cover the whole embryo.
source: In hs-hb; axn RNAi embryos, after a transient down-regulation of mlpt expression, mlpt expression emerged at the posterior then expanded to cover the whole embryo, an effect only observed in the active-zone in WT embryos.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The re-activation of gap gene sequence in Tribolium upon re-inducing hb is specific to the region of the embryo where the posterior morphogen cad is expressed.
source: This supports the hypothesis that the re-activation of gap gene sequence in Tribolium upon re-inducing hb is specific to the region of the embryo where the posterior morphogen cad is expressed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the axn RNAi experiments.

claim: An important class of GRN realizations of the French Flag model exhibits dynamic gene expression patterns and are sensitive to morphogen exposure time, at least during an initial transient phase.
source: In this paper, we argued that an important class of GRN realizations of the FF model exhibits dynamic gene expression patterns and are sensitive to morphogen exposure time, at least during an initial transient phase.
evidence: This is an argument made by the authors based on their computational modeling.

claim: The Speed Regulation model is essentially threshold-free and drives ever-changing gene expression patterns as long as the morphogen gradient is applied.
source: In contrast, the SR model is essentially threshold-free and drives ever-changing gene expression patterns as long as the morphogen gradient is applied.
evidence: This is a description of the Speed Regulation model.

claim: The Speed Regulation and the French Flag with a Timer Gene models are more intimately related than it first appears.
source: In fact, the SR and the FFTG models are more intimately related than it first appears.
evidence: This is an argument made by the authors.

claim: Both the Speed Regulation and the French Flag with a Timer Gene models can be thought of as composed of an 'aperiodic' clock whose speed is regulated by the posterior morphogen.
source: Both models can be thought of as composed of an 'aperiodic' clock whose speed is regulated by the posterior morphogen (grey in Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is an argument made by the authors.

claim: In the Speed Regulation model, the clock is mediated by the regulatory interactions between the fate-specifying genes themselves.
source: In the SR model, the clock is mediated by the regulatory interactions between the fate-specifying genes themselves (e.g. the dynamic module in Figure 1B'').
evidence: This describes the nature of the clock in the Speed Regulation model.

claim: In the French Flag with a Timer Gene model, the clock is the Timer Gene, where each tick of the clock is specified by a different concentration of the Timer Gene.
source: In the FFTG model, the clock is the Timer Gene, where each tick of the clock is specified by a different concentration of the Timer Gene.
evidence: This describes the nature of the clock in the French Flag with a Timer Gene model.

claim: A gene with expression dynamics like that of a Timer Gene has not so far been discovered in insects.
source: Although a gene with expression dynamics like that of a Timer Gene has not so far been discovered in insects, its existence is still a viable possibility.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Resetting the clock of the Speed Regulation model would require resetting the gap gene cascade itself.
source: Resetting the clock of the SR model would, then, requireresetting the gap gene cascade itself, while resetting the clock of the FFTG model would require resetting the Timer Gene.
evidence: This is a prediction from the structure of the Speed Regulation model.

claim: Resetting the clock of the French Flag with a Timer Gene model would require resetting the Timer Gene.
source: Resetting the clock of the SR model would, then, requireresetting the gap gene cascade itself, while resetting the clock of the FFTG model would require resetting the Timer Gene.
evidence: This is a prediction from the structure of the French Flag with a Timer Gene model.

claim: Re-inducing the leading gap gene in the gap gene sequence (hb) in the Tribolium embryo resulted in the re-induction of the gap gene cascade.
source: To investigate whether gap gene regulation in insects are mediated by the SR or the FFTG model, we re-induced the leading gap gene in the gap gene sequence (hb) in the Tribolium embryo, which resulted in the re-induction of the gap gene cascade.
evidence: This is the main experimental finding of the paper.

claim: The experimental observations of re-inducing hb are consistent with a Speed Regulation model of gap gene regulation in Tribolium.
source: These experimental observations are consistent with a Speed Regulation model of gap gene regulation in Tribolium.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Hox genes are expressed sequentially in waves in vertebrates, and are hypothesized to be regulated by a clock mechanism (termed the 'hox clock').
source: Interestingly, hox genes are expressed sequentially in waves in vertebrates, and are hypothesized to be regulated by a clock mechanism (termed the 'hox clock') (Deschamps and Duboule, 2017; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005; Gaunt, 2001).
evidence: This is a statement about hox gene regulation in vertebrates supported by citations.

claim: It is not clear if the hox clock is self-regulatory or regulated by a threshold-based mechanism.
source: It is not clear, however, if this clock is self-regulatory or regulated by a threshold-based mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding the hox clock.

claim: Similar perturbations like the one suggested in this study might resolve whether the hox clock is self-regulatory or threshold-based.
source: Similar perturbations like the one suggested in this study might resolve this issue.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The failure of French Flag GRN to re-induce the patterning genes sequence upon the re-induction of one of the constituent genes is due to the fact that the morphogen gradient is the driving factor behind the sequential activation of genes rather than the cross-regulatory interactions between patterning genes themselves.
source: The failure of FF GRN to re-induce the patterning genes sequence upon the re-induction of one of the constituent genes is due to a general feature of the FF model rather than to some modeling specifics of the used GRNs, namely due to that fact that the morphogen gradient is the driving factor behind the sequential activation of genes rather than the cross-regulatory interactions between patterning genes themselves, as the case in the SR model.
evidence: This is an explanation of why the French Flag model fails to re-induce the patterning sequence.

claim: The dual response of Tribolium embryos upon re-inducing hb supports the two-module realization of the Speed Regulation model.
source: However, the dual response of Tribolium embryos upon re-inducing hb supports the two-module realization (compare Videos 8 and 11).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing experimental results with computational models.

claim: The AC-DC GRN can operate either as a multi-stable circuit (the DC mode) or as a clock (the AC mode), depending on the concentration of a morphogen gradient.
source: The AC-DC GRN can operate either as a multi-stable circuit (the DC mode) or as a clock (the AC mode), depending on the concentration of a morphogen gradient.
evidence: This is a description of the AC-DC GRN from literature.

claim: At certain ranges of the morphogen gradient, both AC and DC modes of the AC-DC GRN could co-exist, resulting in the fine-tuning of the speed of the clock.
source: At certain ranges of the morphogen gradient, both modes could co-exist, resulting in the fine-tuning of the speed of the clock.
evidence: This is a description of the AC-DC GRN behavior.

claim: It is not clear if the AC-DC GRN would be able to mediate a morphogen-mediated transition from the composite AC-DC mode to a pure DC mode to fully realize wavefront-based patterning.
source: However, it is not clear if the AC-DC GRN would be able to mediate a morphogen-mediated transition from the composite AC-DC mode to a pure DC mode to fully realize wavefront-based patterning.
evidence: This is a limitation of the AC-DC GRN noted by the authors.

claim: The AC-DC GRN lacks the flexibility of the two-modules model, since different realizations of the dynamic and static modules in the two-modules model could be employed to mediate a wide range of final spatial patterns without the constraint of using one module to mediate two functions.
source: In addition, while the AC-CD GRN is economical as it uses one module to achieve both AC and DC behaviors, it lacks the flexibility of the two-modules model, since different realizations of the dynamic and static modules in the two-modules model could be employed to mediate a wide range of final spatial patterns without the constraint of using one module to mediate two functions.
evidence: This is a comparison between the AC-DC GRN and the two-modules model.

claim: Gap genes are known to interact with pair-rule genes in Tribolium, albeit a limited interaction.
source: However, gap genes are known to interact with pair-rule genes (albeit a limited interaction in Tribolium (El-Sherif et al., 2012b)).
evidence: This is a statement about gap gene interactions supported by citation.

claim: hb re-activation in the experiments induced the generation of extra segments in cuticles.
source: Indeed, hb re-activation in our experiments induced the generation of extra segments in cuticles (see Appendix 1 for a basic description of cuticlular phenotype of hs-hb experiments).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Depleting hb transcripts by RNAi led to extra segments in the moth Bombyx mori.
source: Interestingly, depleting hb transcripts by RNAi led to extra segments as well in the moth Bombyx mori (Nakao, 2016) (a phenotype that is not observed upon knocking down hb in Tribolium).
evidence: This is a finding from another study cited in the paper.

claim: The extra segments phenotype upon hb depletion in Bombyx mori could be due to a difference in the mode of gap gene regulation between Bombyx and Tribolium or due to the timing of applying RNAi perturbation.
source: However, this could be either due to a difference in the mode of gap gene regulation between the two species or due to the timing of applying RNAi perturbation (as the hb RNAi was done via embryonic injection in Bombyx and via parental injection in Tribolium, leading to the depletion of both maternal and zygotic hb).
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the difference in phenotypes.

claim: The AP fate specification in Tribolium (and possibly other insects) is based on the regulation of an aperiodic clock of gap genes in a threshold-free fashion.
source: In summary, in this paper we showed that the gene expression dynamics driven by a French Flag mechanism can be indistinguishable from those driven by a threshold-free mechanism. We then suggested a test to differentiate between the two cases and carried it out experimentally in the beetle Tribolium castaneum. The test confirmed that the AP fate specification in Tribolium (and possibly other insects) is based on the regulation of an aperiodic clock of gap genes in a threshold-free fashion.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper.
